record.question:
A company runs a public web application on EC2 and wants to improve resilience to network floods and HTTP request floods. Its budget permits CloudFront, AWS WAF, and capacity scaling but not a Shield Advanced subscription.

Which actions directly improve DDoS resilience? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Place CloudFront in front of the application, cache suitable content, restrict direct origin access, and monitor demand with CloudWatch to support controlled Auto Scaling.
Move all application files from EBS to S3 and schedule operating-system patching. Use these changes as the primary protection against request floods.
Distribute allowed HTTP traffic through an Application Load Balancer to a multi-AZ fleet. Associate a WAF web ACL with tested filtering and rate-based rules.
Attach additional network interfaces to each EC2 instance and rely on the extra interfaces to filter malicious requests before they reach the application.
Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances for the existing fleet and rely on the reservation to increase each instance's network capacity during attacks.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<1>> and <<3>>. CloudFront moves request handling to the edge and reduces origin load through caching. WAF filters application-layer requests, while an ALB and a multi-AZ fleet distribute permitted work. Restrict origin access so attackers cannot simply bypass the edge.

<<2>> may improve storage and patch hygiene, but neither change directly filters or absorbs a request flood.

<<4>> does not provide a malicious-request classifier or make instance bandwidth unlimited; network limits still depend on the instance configuration.

<<5>> changes the billing model, not the performance of an otherwise identical instance.

Shield Standard provides automatic baseline protection without a Shield Advanced subscription. WAF rules and application capacity still need tuning. Scaling improves availability but can increase costs and cannot be treated as unlimited attack absorption.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[CloudFront DDoS resilience](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-best-practices-ddos-resiliency/cloudfront.html)
[AWS DDoS mitigation techniques](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-best-practices-ddos-resiliency/mitigation-techniques.html)

diagram_alt: Caching, request filtering, and distributed capacity reduce different parts of the DDoS load.

sources.supports: Edge filtering and caching reduce origin exposure
CloudFront, WAF, ALB, Auto Scaling and baseline mitigation form a layered architecture
